a7f54565c81b: <t1>S143</t1> <t2>Death certificate for Sidsel Kathrine Nielsen Silkjær and Esbjerg’s burial register. The columns “Bopæl (sidste faste Opholdssted)” (residence, last permanent address) and “Dødsstedet” (place of death) are filled in with the same address, Havnegade 152 in Esbjerg — so she died at her home address and not in a hospital. The details of the grave come not from the certificate but from Esbjerg’s burial register: buried 26 May 1938 in the churchyard in Gormsgade, section R, row 13, nos. 17—18; the grave renewed until 1958. Date of death 18 May 1938 at 6 p.m. Principal illness: tuberculosis pulmonum; immediate cause of death given as “Lungetuberkulose” / tb. pulmonum. Certain signs of death: rigor mortis and livor mortis. The certificate issued in Esbjerg on 19 May 1938 by Dr T. Jensen. The occupation column reads “Fhv. Sygeplejerske” (former nurse). The certificate does not say when or why she stopped working, and does not connect the illness with her profession</t2>

36a67e656d15: <t1>S149</t1> <t2>Genealogical record of Esper Nielsen Silkjær’s family — extract from a table of descendants, compiled around 2009 (it refers to two of the children as “endnu lever (2009)”, still living in 2009), received August 2026. It gives the marriage on 17 March 1913 in Gudum, the farm Nørre Tangshus as the home of the couple and the children, their old age at Fredensgade 11 in Struer and eight children with dates of birth and baptism from the Gudum parish register; the entries have not been checked in the original. On Knud Vognsgaard: employed on 26 April 1953 as a smelter at the steelworks in Frederiksværk, killed in the explosion there on 27 May 1959, buried on 31 May in Skævinge; married to Ebba Ruth Nielsen, left a wife and three children — the disaster is independently confirmed by the obituary in the folk high school’s alumni magazine [S150] and by Halsnæs Municipality’s cultural heritage analysis [S151]; press reports and the death certificate have not been traced, and the course of events itself has not been reconstructed. The family file [S40] spells the middle name Vagnsgaard, where the record writes Vognsgaard; the parish register has not been consulted. Of Alma the record writes “aldrig gift” (never married), while the family file lists a marriage — the contradiction has not been resolved, and the chronicle takes no position. The children’s years and places of death (Niels 1999 in Struer, Krista 2006 in a care home on Amager, Alma 2013 at Svendborg hospital, Helga 2004 in Arnborg — the record says Herning, near which Arnborg lies) follow the family file; Otto’s emigration to Australia and his death rest on the record alone</t2>
e9d1108ff8f0: <t1>S150</t1> <t2>Nr. Nissum Folk High School alumni magazine, no. 6, June 1959 (skolehistorie.dk) — obituary of Knud Vognsgaard Silkjær, winter student 1933/34, with a portrait photograph, reproduced as image 54. Written by his sister, who signs “Ane Pedersen, f. Silkjær (1938)” — herself a former student; the signature independently confirms the record’s [S149] marriage between Ane Kristiane and Thorvald Pedersen. The text opens “Onsdag den 27. maj fik vi det tunge budskab, at vor kære broder Knud var død som følge af den store ulykke på Frederiksværk Stålvalseværk” (On Wednesday 27 May we received the heavy news that our dear brother Knud had died as a result of the great disaster at the Frederiksværk steelworks) — 27 May 1959 was a Wednesday — and records a wife and three children aged 19, 16 and 8, “et dejligt hus med have” (a lovely house with a garden) in Skævinge, the daily drive to the works in Frederiksværk and the family’s last meeting with him at Easter, “da han var hjemme i Struer med familien” (when he was at home in Struer with the family) — with his parents Esper and Jensine, cf. S149. The school’s own addition: “Han var så ung og så glad og fornøjelig. Havde vi ikke haft ham på vinterholdet for 25 år siden, så havde der ligesom manglet noget væsentligt.” (He was so young and so cheerful and good company. Had we not had him in the winter class 25 years ago, something essential would have been missing.) The magazine spells the town “Skævingen”. Nørre Nissum Folk High School was the Inner Mission’s first folk high school in Denmark, founded in 1887 by the parish priest Ad. L. Hansen in collaboration with the Inner Mission’s board and Vilhelm Beck — cf. the school’s anniversary publications of 1937, 1962 and 1987, in the same place</t2>
68f985c8c679: <t1>S151</t1> <t2>Analysis of Frederiksværk’s industrial heritage — preliminary analysis for Stålsat By (Steel-set Town), Halsnæs Municipality (halsnaes.dk) — on Det Danske Staalvalseværk: “Det var ikke nogen sikker arbejdsplads. I 1959 mistede fem arbejdere livet og mange andre fik skader for livet, efter en stor eksplosion.” (It was not a safe workplace. In 1959 five workers lost their lives and many others were injured for life after a great explosion.) The same analysis sets out the scale of the works in the 1950s: almost 1,000 employees and an annual steel production of 110,000 tons, the country’s largest recycling plant. The analysis does not date the explosion more closely; the day, 27 May, comes from the genealogical record [S149] and is confirmed by the alumni magazine [S150]</t2>

cf292480c22d: <t1>S155</t1> <t2>The National Museum of Denmark, history of fashion, “Hvid brudekjole — chemisekjole ca. 1797” (White wedding dress — chemise dress c. 1797) (natmus.dk): “Blandt bønder og den jævne del af bybefolkningen har sort brudekjole været det mest almindelige. Det var ikke kun et spørgsmål om økonomi, men også om tradition” (among farmers and the ordinary part of the town population the black wedding dress was the most common; it was not only a question of money but also of tradition) — white was for “de fine” (the gentry). Magasin du Nord Museum, the exhibition “Det er så yndigt”: in the nineteenth century most Danish brides were married in a simple black dress, sewn for the occasion, which would afterwards serve as the best party dress; only around 1920 did white become the dominant colour for wedding dresses</t2>

49de2badf5e2: <t1>S169</t1> <t2>Journal 1859—1943, Vridsløselille State Prison (vols. 77—80, 1910—1919) — the entries on the refusal of the petition for pardon for prisoner no. 240 (forwarded by the Director of Prisons 17—19 July 1913) and on the recommendation on 10 November 1913 of seven prisoners for pardon on the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the House of Glücksburg’s reign, with the endorsement “15/11-13 Dir. medd. Kgl. R. af 15/11 13: alle syv benaadede … Alle løsl. 15/11 13” (15/11-13 the Director reports royal resolution of 15/11 13: all seven pardoned … all released 15/11 13). 6b2ee8b0b3a2: <t1>S170</t1> <t2>Letter book 1859—1943, Vridsløselille State Prison (vols. 7—8, 1912—1920) — letter no. 131 of 10 November 1913 to the Director of Prisons: the recommendation of seven prisoners for the jubilee pardon, among them “No 240 Fisker Thomas Nielsen Silkjær” with the characterisation “Han opfører sig godt og synes at angre sin Forbrydelse. I Hjemmet savnes han haardt” (He conducts himself well and seems to repent of his crime. He is sorely missed at home) and the reference to the judge’s recommendation of the petition refused in July. Danish National Archives, Viborg; photographed 12 August 2026</t2>
61f6f6a659dd: <t1>S171</t1> <t2>Niels Iversen Klit, “Husby Klit — en egnsskildring fra gammel tid” (Husby Klit — a local account from olden times), no. 8 — summary of the parish board meeting at Husby rectory on 15 April 1846: Jens Claus Mattzen, for whom discharge from school was requested, was examined in arithmetic with a satisfactory result, and the discharge was granted; the request had been submitted too late and should have been made immediately after the autumn examination. The booklet adds that the foreign-looking spelling of the surname was probably due to Jens Claus having been born and baptised in Angeln in South Schleswig. The booklet is probably based on the parish board’s minute book</t2>
3affc428bf0d: <t1>S172</t1> <t2>Parish register for Nysogn (Haurvig church district), births 1893, no. 10 — Søren Mathiasen Pedersen Heide, born 17 November 1893 at Bjerregaard, son of the smallholder Anders Hejde Pedersen and his wife Edel Kirstine Hansen, 27, Bjerregaard; baptised in Haurvig Church on Boxing Day by Pastor Alfred Jørgensen, the mother carrying the child herself, godparents the smallholders Peder Lodbjerg, Laust Kristensen and Søren Thomas Hansen, all of Bjerregaard. “Heide” in the child’s name is in paler ink and was added later: the family received Heide as an official surname by licence of 21 August 1905</t2>
9132394be1b8: <t1>S173</t1> <t2>Ringkøbing town bailiff: case files (1913) — Ringkjøbing County’s letter of 31 March 1913 from Rindumgaard, the county’s case number D 698 with a printed request that the number be given in letters concerning the case, and the endorsement “Arrestantsag” (prisoner case): in connection with the transcript of examinations received with the chief of police’s letter of the 28th of the same month, notice is given that proceedings were brought the same day against Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen for breach of § 162 of the Penal Code, and that the barrister Grove and the solicitor Kamp have been appointed to conduct the case, “den førstnævnte som Aktor, den sidstnævnte som Defensor” (the former as prosecutor, the latter as defence counsel); the defence is asked to be given the necessary notice of the above. Signed by the county governor — H.C. Dons, governor of Ringkjøbing County 1903—15, residing at Rindumgaard, cf. Kraks Vejviser 1913. At the bottom the district office’s red journal endorsement 48/13; the offices of town bailiff and district bailiff were combined. Danish National Archives, Viborg; photographed 13 August 2026. Reproduced as image 60</t2>
8d31589aebdd: <t1>S174</t1> <t2>St Michael’s Church, Fredericia — the biography of Carl Marius Hornbech (1871—1934) on the board of priests, compiled by the historical consultant Ole Dyrn (sctm.dk): a priest’s son, schooled at Randers Latin School, cand.theol. 1896, YMCA secretary in Aarhus 1898, ordained assistant in Copenhagen 1899, missionary in India from 1902 — where his first wife Olga died in 1908 — travelling preacher for the Danish Missionary Society from 1909 and parish priest in Fredericia St Michael-Erritsø 1915—34. Supplemented by Dansk Forfatterleksikon (danskforfatterleksikon.dk) and by the school programmes for the preparatory school to the State School in Randers 1912—14 (skolehistorie.dk), which list among the pupils a child with the father given as “Hornbech (Præst)” — so a Pastor Hornbech with children at school lived in Randers in exactly those years</t2>
98198b0e2348: <t1>S175</t1> <t2>Information given to the chronicle by Annette’s family, August 2026 — on the adoption, the nursing training, the move to Copenhagen during her training, the two children, the presumed absence of contact with her biological father and her death in 2024, shortly after her eightieth birthday, which was celebrated with the family in her daughter’s garden. The informant is known to the chronicle but is not named</t2>
c4d02546db6a: <t1>S176</t1> <t2>The criminal file in the case against Thomas Nielsen Silkjær and Christine Oline Enevoldsen — Ringkøbing Police, box B-410, folder no. 408: “Aktor, Overretssagfører Grove ctr. Thomas Nielsen Silkjær og Christine Oline Enevoldsen”, county journal no. D 698 – 1913. Contents: the transcript of the judgment book “in forma” with endorsements of service and execution; Grove’s summons of 1 April and submission of 2 April 1913; Kamp’s submission of 9 April 1913; a certified transcript of the examinations in the police record book (24 and 28 February, 7, 17, 22 and 26 March) with the county’s order of prosecution of 31 March; and exhibits A—K: the police report of 17 February (A), the arrest requisition of 18 February (B), the transcript of the Copenhagen Criminal and Police Court’s examination no. 575 of 21 February (C), the telegram about the arrest (D), certificates of baptism for Thomas and Christine (E, F), the marriage certificate (G), the midwife’s certificate of 10 March (H) and the certificates of criminal record (I, K). Danish National Archives; photographs received and transcribed on 26 August 2026. See caveat 32</t2>
5d94d1052b93: <t1>S177</t1> <t2>Politiets Efterretninger (the Police Gazette) 1913, no. 23 (22 February) and no. 24 (25 February) — the arrest of Thomas Nielsen Silkjær (Husby, 10/1 82) for breach of § 162 of the Penal Code in another jurisdiction, listed under “Anholdte for Forbrydelser m. v.” (arrested for crimes etc.), and the transfer under “Afgivne til frem. 4b0169f3c455: <t1>S179</t1> <t2>Torben Klinting, “Fiskerne fra Nymindegab” (The fishermen of Nymindegab) — the account of the disaster of 1 April 1896: the five names of the boat’s crew with position and civil status, the ownership of “Forsøget” and the two young farmhands’ wages, the putting out on the afternoon of 31 March, the course of the wreck, Søren Andersen Jensen drifting on an oar and his rescue by Enevold Enevoldsen with a line round his waist, Peder Enevoldsen drifting on a stump of mast, the beach bailiff Jens Dahl’s finding of the three bodies off Gødelen on Maundy Thursday, the funerals in Haurvig, Nr. Lyngvig and Sdr. Bork, the stranding of the wreck off Hovstrup, the rescue medal to Enevold Enevoldsen and the inscription on the memorial stone. Received as a transcript on 7 September 2026 from Hardy Sørensen, the Archive in Fiskeriets Hus, Hvide Sande; page number not given, the book not seen. See caveat 46</t2>
cbfe044fdc44: <t1>S180</t1> <t2>Dagens Nyheder, 28 May 1896, “Mindestøtte over druknede Fiskere” (Memorial to drowned fishermen) — reported from Ringkjøbing Avis: the unveiling of the memorial stone on Whit Sunday, the stone’s place close to the road in Aargab village on a fenced plot given by Knud Andersen, the inscription with the four names, c. 500 present, the gunboat “Grønsund” with its commander Captain Brædstrup and First Lieutenant Reinhardt, “Dejlig er Jorden” (Fair is the Earth) at 3 o’clock and the handing over of the stone from the fishermen of Esbjerg to those of the dunes. Received as a transcript on 7 September 2026 from Hardy Sørensen; the newspaper page has not been seen, and the quotation is given in the transcript’s spelling</t2>
1307107a18a1: <t1>S181</t1> <t2>Søren Rinder Kristensen, Årgab, account of Ane Marie Enevoldsen (1868—1953) — Peder Enevoldsen’s widow, the children Jensigne (b. 1893) and Kresten, the house at Årgab, her son’s drowning in Ringkøbing Fjord in March 1918 together with Peder Sand and Ole Madsen, her old age with her daughter in Alslev and the grave in Haurvig churchyard. Written down by the author, with additions from Hardy Sørensen. The author is the grandson of the survivor Søren Andersen Jensen and gives the family tradition that his grandfather was saved on an oar. Family tradition, not archival records. See caveat 48</t2>
